newsitem.title: FRANCE: Solana backs east-west NATO summit plan.
newsitem.headline: Solana backs east-west NATO summit plan.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Monday promised France a major role in the Atlantic Alliance command structure once it returns to full integration into NATO's military wing, which it left in 1966.

Solana endorsed calls by French President Jacques Chirac and the United States for a summit of NATO's 16 nations and east European candidates for membership with Russia in mid-1997 to approve a new security architecture for Europe.

He also made clear he expected Western peacekeeping troops to stay in Bosnia after the NATO-led peace implementation force's mandate expires at the end of the year, saying he hoped the international community would not abandon Bosnia.

"France's role will be very, very important. It must play a role proportionate to its capabilities and its importance," Solana told reporters after talks with Chirac which he described as very constructive.
"I hope we will be able to find a solution so that France as well as Spain, which are moving closer to NATO, can be comfortable in the new command structure," he said.

Diplomatic sources said France is in tough negotiations with both its European allies and the United States on the role of the Western European Union defence grouping, and of French officers, in a reformed NATO military wing.

Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said the president had stressed the need for practical arrangements "to give the necessary political visibility and operational capability to a European defence identity".

French Defence Minister Charles Millon called this month for the appointment of a European deputy to the U.S. Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), who would command WEU military operations in which the United States chose not to participate.

The diplomats said Paris sought that role for itself and was also interested in one of NATO's major regional commands in Europe. At present the three area commands are held by British, German and U.S. officers.

The Naples-based post of commander-in-chief of allied forces in southern Europe, now held by a U.S. admiral, interests the French, but Washington wants to keep it tied to command of the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean, the diplomats said.

The newspaper Liberation said on Monday that Paris had dismissed the offer of a new southwest European command covering its own territory, the Iberian peninsula and the Atlantic approaches, saying nothing ever happened there.
Solana said he and Chirac discussed the issue of France's place in the NATO command structure but gave no details.
General Charles de Gaulle pulled France out of the alliance's military wing in 1966 in protest at U.S. domination.

Chirac took the first step toward returning to full participation last year when he agreed to allow France's defence minister and chief of staff to attend NATO meetings for the first time in three decades.
The diplomats said that beyond the ambitions of French generals, at issue was the degree of autonomy which European forces would have in running their own security operations.
On NATO enlargement, Solana said he hoped a final decision would be taken at the summit in mid-1997.
The NATO chief and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov came no closer to compromise on Friday on NATO's plans, opposed by Moscow, to admit ex-Soviet bloc states as members.

However, Colonna said Chirac had noted there was now broad support for the idea of "a new organisation of peace on the European continent", which could take the form of a NATO pact with Russia to wipe out the effects of the 1945 Yalta division of Europe and avoid creating new fault lines.
